questions.q: What is a logical partition in Cosmos DB?
options: The set of all items sharing the same partition key value — Cosmos DB's internal unit of data distribution
A physical server dedicated to a single container
A backup copy of a container
A deprecated concept no longer used in Cosmos DB
questions.explain: Items with the same partition key value form one logical partition, which Cosmos DB then automatically maps onto physical partitions.

questions.q: Who manages the mapping of logical partitions onto physical partitions?
options: Cosmos DB does this automatically and transparently
The DBA manually creates and assigns each physical partition
It requires a separate Azure resource to be provisioned manually
Physical partitions do not exist in Cosmos DB
questions.explain: Unlike manually configuring MongoDB shard servers, a DBA never manually manages physical partitions — Cosmos DB handles that mapping automatically.

questions.q: Why is a partition key like `orderStatus` (five possible values) a poor choice for a large container?
options: Low cardinality caps the number of logical partitions that can ever exist, capping scalability regardless of provisioned throughput
orderStatus is not a valid JSON property name
Cosmos DB requires partition keys to be numeric
It would cause data loss immediately upon container creation
questions.explain: With only five possible values, at most five logical partitions could ever exist — a hard ceiling on distribution, mirroring low-cardinality shard key problems in MongoDB.

options: A logical partition receiving disproportionate request volume, getting throttled independently of other partitions
The physical partition storing the most recently created items
A partition that has been manually marked as high-priority
A partition key value that no longer exists in the container
questions.explain: Even distribution of request volume matters as much as cardinality — one overloaded value creates a hot, throttled partition while others sit idle.

questions.q: Why is discovering a bad partition key choice after production data has accumulated expensive to fix?
options: The partition key path is fixed for the life of a container, so fixing it requires creating a new container and migrating all the data
Cosmos DB allows changing the partition key with a single command at no cost
It isn't expensive — partition keys can be edited freely at any time
It requires deleting the entire Cosmos DB account
questions.explain: This mirrors the real cost of a bad MongoDB shard key — both require a genuine data migration, not an in-place edit, once the collection or container holds production data.
